### CHAPTER 13: SAFE WORK PRACTICES AND PROCEDURES

This chapter consolidates the day-to-day safe work practices that apply across all departments on set. It is not a substitute for the detailed requirements in Chapters 1 through 12; rather, it is a practical reference for common situations. Where a conflict exists between this chapter and a specific chapter, the more specific requirement governs.

#### 13.1 General Work Practices

All crew members, regardless of department, must follow these basic rules when working near electrical equipment:

1.  Assume every conductor is energized until it has been verified de-energized with a tested meter.
2.  Do not wear loose clothing, dangling jewelry, or unsecured long hair when working on or near energized equipment.
3.  Remove all conductive items from your pockets (e.g., metal tools, tape measures, keys) before reaching into any panel or junction box.
4.  Use only insulated tools rated for the voltage level on which you are working.
5.  Never work alone on energized equipment. A second person must be within sight or hearing range and know how to shut off power and call for help.
6.  Do not use damaged or frayed cords, cables, or connectors. Tag them out of service immediately and report them to the Best Boy Electric.
7.  Keep all work areas clean and dry. Water and electricity do not mix. If a spill occurs near electrical equipment, stop work, control the spill, and notify the Electric Department.

> **WARNING:** The use of "cheater" cords, ungrounded adapters, or any device that defeats the grounding prong on a plug is strictly prohibited. This is a direct violation of this manual and may result in immediate removal from the electrical crew.

#### 13.2 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedures

Lockout/Tagout is required before any work is performed on equipment that could be accidentally energized. This includes distribution equipment, generators, and any fixed electrical installation used in support of production.

The authorized employee performing the work is responsible for applying their own lock and tag. The Best Boy Electric must be notified before any LOTO is applied, except in an emergency.

**Procedure:**

1.  Notify all affected crew members that power will be shut off and why.
2.  Identify all energy sources, including backup sources and stored energy (e.g., capacitors).
3.  Shut off the equipment using normal operating controls.
4.  Apply the lock and tag at the disconnecting means. Each person working on the equipment must have their own lock.
5.  Attempt to restart the equipment to verify it is de-energized. Return the controls to the "Off" position after the test.
6.  Verify the absence of voltage with a tested meter before beginning work.
7.  When work is complete, remove all tools and guards, replace all covers, and ensure all crew members are clear.
8.  Remove the lock and tag only after the work is complete and the equipment is ready to be returned to service.

## Chapter 14: Training Program and Certification Requirements

### 14.1 Overview of the Training Program

The Basic Electrical Safety Manual serves as the primary resource for all electrical safety training conducted by the Electric Department. This chapter outlines the training curriculum, assessment methods, and certification requirements for all crew members who work with or around electrical equipment on production.

All crew members, regardless of experience level, must complete the training program before being assigned to work on electrical systems. This includes not only set electricians but also grips, camera operators, and any other department personnel who may come into contact with electrical equipment during the course of their work.

The training program is designed to be practical and hands-on. Classroom instruction is kept to a minimum, with the majority of learning taking place on the set or in the shop. The program follows the structure of this manual, with each chapter corresponding to a training module.

### 14.2 Training Modules

The training program is divided into ten modules, each covering a major topic area from the manual. Modules are typically completed in order, although crew members with prior experience may test out of early modules with the approval of the Best Boy Electric or the Gaffer.

**Module 1: Introduction to Electrical Safety**  
- Chapter 1 of the manual  
- Topics covered: The importance of electrical safety, common hazards on set, and the role of the Electric Department  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction  
- Assessment: Written quiz (20 questions, 80% to pass)

**Module 2: Electrical Theory Fundamentals**  
- Chapter 2 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Basic concepts of voltage, current, resistance, and power; AC vs. DC systems; and how electricity behaves in different conditions  
- Duration: 4 hours of classroom instruction  
- Assessment: Written quiz (25 questions, 80% to pass)

**Module 3: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**  
- Chapter 3 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Selection, inspection, and proper use of PPE, including gloves, safety glasses, and arc-rated clothing  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction plus 2 hours of hands-on practice  
- Assessment: Practical demonstration of proper PPE selection and donning

**Module 4: Working with Distribution Equipment**  
- Chapter 4 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Distribution panels, feeder cables, connectors, and proper setup and teardown procedures  
- Duration: 8 hours of hands-on training in the shop or on a stage  
- Assessment: Practical skills test with a checklist evaluation

**Module 5: Generators and Portable Power**  
- Chapter 5 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Generator safety, fueling procedures, grounding, and load management  
- Duration: 4 hours of classroom instruction plus 4 hours of hands-on training  
- Assessment: Written quiz plus practical demonstration of generator setup and shutdown

**Module 6: Lighting Equipment Safety**  
- Chapter 6 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Safe handling of lighting units, lamp replacement, and working at height  
- Duration: 4 hours of hands-on training  
- Assessment: Practical skills test with a checklist evaluation

**Module 7: Cable Management and Protection**  
- Chapter 7 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Proper cable routing, protection methods, and avoiding damage to cables  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction plus 2 hours of hands-on practice  
- Assessment: Written quiz (15 questions, 80% to pass)

**Chapter 9: Change Management and Manual Maintenance**

This chapter explains how the manual is kept current. It describes the process for proposing changes, the roles of the people who review them, and how approved changes become part of the official document. The goal is to make sure the manual reflects real working conditions on our productions, incorporates lessons learned from incidents and near-misses, and stays aligned with relevant regulations and industry best practices.

**9.1 Why the Manual Changes**

The manual is not a static document. It changes because the work changes. New equipment comes into the rental house, a production site reveals an unanticipated hazard, a crew member identifies a clearer way to describe a procedure, or a regulatory body issues an updated standard. Each of these situations can lead to a change request.

Anyone who works with the manual—set electricians, best boys, gaffers, trainees, safety officers, or producers—can identify a need for change. The process described below is designed to be accessible. You do not need special permission to propose a change. You only need to describe the problem clearly and suggest a fix (if you have one in mind).

**9.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

Several groups and individuals have specific roles in the change management process.

**9.2.1 Manual Owner**

The Manual Owner is the person responsible for the overall content, structure, and accuracy of the manual. This role is currently held by the Safety & Training Coordinator (M. Chen). The Manual Owner:

- Maintains the master copy of the manual and its revision history.
- Assigns version numbers and controls the release schedule.
- Reviews all change requests for technical accuracy and consistency with the rest of the manual.
- Decides whether a change request is accepted, rejected, or sent back for more information.
- Ensures that approved changes are incorporated into the next version of the manual.
- Coordinates with the Training Committee when a change affects training modules, quizzes, or hands-on assessments.

The Manual Owner does not act alone. Substantive changes (those that affect procedures, safety requirements, or training) are reviewed by the Training Committee before final approval. Minor editorial corrections (for example, fixing a typo or clarifying a sentence without changing the meaning) can be handled directly by the Manual Owner.

**General Safety Principles**
- Treat every circuit as live until you have verified it is de-energized with your own test instrument.
- Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is mandatory before working on any circuit that could be energized by another person.
- Only qualified persons may work on exposed energized parts. A qualified person is defined in Section 3.2.
- When in doubt, stop work and ask the Best Boy Electric or Gaffer. There is no penalty for asking a question.

**Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**
- Class 00 rubber gloves (with leather protectors) are the minimum for any work near exposed conductors below 500 V AC.
- Arc-rated face shields are required when there is a risk of arc flash. See the arc flash boundary table in Section 4.4.
- Insulated tools with the appropriate rating must be used on or near energized equipment.
- PPE must be inspected before each use. Gloves must be air-tested per the manufacturer's instructions.

**Grounding and Bonding**
- The grounding conductor is a safety path, not a current-carrying conductor under normal conditions.
- Bonding jumpers must be sized according to Table 5.2 and attached to verified grounds.
- A ground fault is any unintentional flow of current to ground. GFCIs and equipment grounding are the primary protections.
- Never remove the grounding prong from a plug to make it fit an outlet.

**Generator Safety**
- Generators must be placed on level ground, with adequate ventilation and a minimum clearance from combustible materials as specified in Section 6.3.
- The neutral-to-ground bond must be verified before connecting any distribution equipment.
- Fueling must be done with the generator off and cool. No smoking within 20 feet of the fueling area.
- Always use a bonding whip when connecting a generator to a distribution system that relies on the generator as the separately derived source.

**Distribution and Cable Management**
- Feeder cables must be protected from vehicular traffic with cable ramps or by routing them overhead.
- Overhead cable crossings must have a minimum clearance of 14 feet over roadways and 10 feet over walkways (Section 7.4).
- All connections must be made with the appropriate connectors. Never use tape to make a splice on feeder cable.
- Cable that shows signs of cuts, abrasion, or heat damage must be removed from service and tagged for repair.

**Special Equipment**
- Lighting systems, including LED fixtures, must be bonded and grounded per Chapter 8.
- Ballasts and drivers must be inspected for cracked housings or loose connections before use.
- Work lights placed near water or damp locations must be GFCI-protected and rated for damp locations.

**Emergency Procedures**
- In the event of an electric shock, do not touch the victim until the power is de-energized.
- Call 911 immediately. Administer CPR if you are trained and the scene is safe.
- Use a Class C fire extinguisher on electrical fires. Do not use water.
- Report all incidents, including near misses, to the Safety Officer within 24 hours.

1. Confirm generator placement and clearance.
   - Generator is on level, compacted ground or on the specified pad. Not blocking an exit, a hydrant, or a driveway that the production office has flagged as active.
   - Minimum 3 ft clearance on the exhaust side and 2 ft on all other sides. If the generator is inside a tent or under a canopy, the canopy must be fire-rated and the exhaust must be ducted outside.
   - Reference: Manual Section 2.1, Generator Placement.

2. Check the generator fuel level and record it in the fuel log.
   - Minimum 1/4 tank before starting. If below that, note it on the fuel log and order a delivery before you proceed.
   - Confirm the fuel type matches the generator's label (diesel, gasoline, or propane). Do not mix.
   - Reference: Manual Section 2.3, Fuel Handling.

3. Inspect the generator's grounding electrode.
   - The copper ground rod is driven at least 8 ft into the ground, within 6 ft of the generator frame.
   - The ground cable from the generator frame to the rod is #6 AWG or larger, and the connection at the rod is clean, tight, and protected from weather with a rated clamp.
   - If the ground rod is missing or the cable is damaged, stop and call the best boy. Do not substitute a water pipe or a fence post.
   - Reference: Manual Section 3.1, Grounding.

4. Verify the generator output voltage and phase configuration.
   - Check the label on the generator head and the selector switch position. Confirm it matches the distro box rating (120/208 or 120/240).
   - If the production is running a 480 V feed, the generator must be a 480 V unit, not a step-up transformer on a 208 V generator. Step-up transformers are not allowed on this production.
   - Reference: Manual Section 4.2, Voltage Configuration.

The Generator Hookup Checklist specifies a required_item_count of 12. Record status: current.

5. Confirm the distro box is de-energized and locked out.
   - The main breaker on the distro box is in the OFF position.
   - The lockout/tagout device is in place with your name and the date on the tag.
   - If the distro box is fed from another source (e.g., a building panel), that source is also locked out and tagged.
   - Reference: Manual Section 5.1, Lockout/Tagout.

6. Inspect the feeder cable from the generator to the distro box.
   - Cable is rated for the generator's full output, not less than the ampacity on the distro box label.
   - No cuts, abrasions, or exposed copper along the entire length. Pay extra attention to the ends and any point where the cable crosses a road or walkway.
   - If the cable runs across a road, it is protected by cable ramps rated for the heaviest vehicle on the lot.
   - Reference: Manual Section 6.2, Feeder Cable Inspection.

7. Make the connection at the distro box.
   - With the generator OFF, land the three phase conductors and the neutral on the correct lugs. Torque to the value printed on the lug or in the distro box lid.
   - The ground conductor is connected to the ground bus, not the neutral bus, unless the distro box is a separately derived system. When in doubt, ask the best boy before energizing.
   - Reference: Manual Section 7.1, Distro Box Connections.

8. Make the connection at the generator.
   - With the generator OFF, connect the output cables to the generator terminals in the same phase order as the distro box. The neutral is connected to the generator's neutral lug.
   - Verify the phase rotation matches between the generator and the distro box. If you are unsure, mark the cables with tape before you disconnect anything.
   - Reference: Manual Section 7.3, Generator Output Terminals.

9. Check the condition of the cam-type connectors (if used).
   - Each connector is clean, free of corrosion, and the locking collar engages fully.
   - The color bands on the connectors match the phase color on the cable (black, red, blue for 120/208; brown, orange, yellow for 120/240).
   - Replace any connector that is cracked or has a loose fit. Do not tape over a damaged connector.

# Using the Generator Hookup Checklist

## Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1: Confirm You Have the Correct Version

Before starting any work, verify that the copy of the checklist you are holding is **Version 1.7** with a last-updated date of **2025-10-28**. Check the header on every page. If you are using a printed copy from a binder or a toolbox, confirm it matches the current version posted in the electrical staging area. If there is any doubt, print a fresh copy from the shared drive. Do not rely on memory for version numbers.

### Step 2: Review the Entire Checklist Before Touching Equipment

Read through all items on the checklist once, from start to finish, before you begin the physical hookup. This is not a suggestion; it is a requirement. The checklist is arranged in the order work should be performed, but reading it through first helps you spot anything unusual about the specific generator or location you are working with. If you see an item that does not apply to your situation, do not skip it silently. Flag it to the best boy electric or the Electrical Department head before proceeding.

### Step 3: Gather Required Equipment and PPE

Before approaching the generator, ensure you have:

- Class 0 rubber gloves (rated for the voltage you are working with)
- Leather protectors worn over the rubber gloves
- Safety glasses or face shield
- Hard hat (required in all staging areas)
- Voltage-rated lockout/tagout kit with your personal lock
- Multimeter with probes rated for the circuit voltage
- Flashlight (even for daytime work, in case you are working in a shaded or enclosed area)

Do not begin the checklist until you have all of these items. If any piece of PPE is missing or damaged, stop and report it. Do not substitute equipment that is not rated for the job.

### Step 4: Position the Generator

The first items on the checklist (Items 1 through 4) cover generator placement. Follow them in order:

- Confirm the generator is on level ground. If it is not, use cribbing or pads as directed by the best boy electric. Do not use scrap wood from the set.
- Verify clearance on all sides. The minimum clearance is specified in the checklist. If you are in a tight location, such as a backlot alley or a narrow street, measure the clearance rather than eyeballing it.
- Confirm the exhaust is directed away from doors, windows, and air intake vents. This includes vents on adjacent buildings, not just the structure you are shooting in.
- Check that the generator's access panels and control panel are reachable and unobstructed. You will need to access these during startup and shutdown.

### Step 5: Perform the Pre-Connection Inspection

Items 5 through 9 cover the generator itself. These steps are quick but critical:

- Walk around the generator once and look for fluid leaks, loose panels, or anything that looks out of place. If you see a leak, do not proceed. Report it immediately.
- Check the fuel level and record it in the appropriate log. The checklist has a space for this. If the fuel level is below the marked line, arrange for a fuel delivery before you continue.
- Verify that all circuit breakers on the generator are in the OFF position. This includes the main breaker and any branch breakers.
- Confirm that the emergency stop button is not depressed and is functioning. Test it according to the manufacturer's instructions if you are trained to do so. If you are not trained on that specific generator model, ask the best boy electric to demonstrate it.
- Inspect the condition of the output cables. Look for cuts, abrasions, or exposed conductors. Pay special attention to the ends where the connectors attach. If any cable shows damage, tag it out of service and do not use it.
**ELECTRIC DEPARTMENT TRAINING MEMO – REV 4**

**To:** All Electric Department Trainees and Working Electricians
**From:** Daniel Okafor, Department Head Electric
**Date:** March 14, 2026
**Re:** Generator Hookup Checklist – Training Program Integration and Assessment

---

This memo covers how the Generator Hookup Checklist (latest revision: March 2026, Rev 4) is used in the electric department training program. It is not a substitute for the checklist itself. You are expected to have a copy of the checklist with you during all training exercises and on any job where a generator hookup is part of your assigned duties.

The training program is divided into three phases. The checklist is introduced in Phase 1, practiced in Phase 2, and assessed in Phase 3. Each phase has its own requirements and sign-off procedures. If you are reading this memo as a returning electrician who has been away from the department for more than twelve months, you are required to complete Phase 2 refresher exercises before you can work on a generator without direct supervision.

---

### Phase 1: Classroom Introduction

Phase 1 is a two-day classroom session. On the first day, you will receive a copy of the Generator Hookup Checklist and the instructor will walk through each item in order. You are expected to follow along and mark up your copy with notes. The instructor will cover the reasons behind each item, including the relevant code references and department policies. You do not need to memorize the checklist in Phase 1, but you do need to be able to explain why each item exists.

On the second day, the instructor will review common mistakes and near-miss reports from the last two years. The checklist was updated in part because of those reports. For example, Item 12 (verify the bonding conductor is connected before the main breaker is closed) was added after a 2024 incident where a crew hooked up a generator without the bonding conductor and did not catch it until the first load test. That incident is covered in the training slides. Pay attention to those slides; the examples are frequently used in the Phase 3 assessment.

At the end of Phase 1, you will take a short written quiz. The quiz has ten questions. Five of the questions ask you to identify the correct order of the first five checklist items. The other five ask you to match a checklist item to the reason it exists. You must score at least eight out of ten to pass. If you do not pass, you will retake the quiz on the third day. You can retake it as many times as needed within the training week, but each retake is a different version of the quiz.

---

### Phase 2: Hands-On Practice

Phase 2 is a half-day practical session. It is held on the backlot, in the area behind Stage 4. You will work in pairs. One person is the lead electrician and the other is the assistant. The instructor assigns the roles. After the first exercise, you swap roles.

You will complete two generator hookups from start to finish. The first hookup uses a 60 kW towable generator. The second uses a 150 kW trailer-mounted unit. The instructor will observe you and mark a copy of the checklist as you work. The instructor does not prompt you. If you skip a step, the instructor notes it and you continue. At the end of the exercise, the instructor reviews the marked checklist with you and goes over any skipped or incorrect items.

The purpose of Phase 2 is to build muscle memory, not to test you. You are expected to make mistakes. The instructor will point them out and you will correct them before the next exercise. If you have questions during the exercise, you may ask, but the instructor will not answer questions about the order of the checklist. That is part of the assessment.

- **Qualified Person:** An individual who has received documented training in the hazards of electrical work and has demonstrated proficiency in the tasks assigned.
- **Lockout/Tagout (LOTO):** A procedure to ensure that equipment is de-energized and secured against accidental re-energization before work begins.
- **GFCI (Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupter):** A device that interrupts electrical current when a ground fault is detected.
- **Feeder:** A cable or conductor that carries power from a source to a distribution point.

**4. Responsibilities**

- Maintains and updates this manual.
- Approves all revisions.
- Conducts periodic audits of electrical practices.

**4.2 Set Electricians**

- Comply with all requirements of this manual.
- Report any unsafe condition or near-miss incident to the Best Boy Electric or Safety Officer.
- Ensure that all equipment used is inspected and in good working order.

**4.3 Trainees**

- Work under the direct supervision of a Qualified Person.
- Complete all required training modules before performing unsupervised tasks.

**4.4 Evaluators**

- Assess trainee competency using the checklists referenced in Chapter 10.
- Provide feedback to trainees and to the training coordinator.

**5. General Safety Rules**

1. Only Qualified Persons may perform electrical work.
2. Assume all conductors are energized until verified de-energized.
3. Use lockout/tagout procedures whenever working on de-energized circuits.
4. All temporary power distribution must include GFCI protection where required.
5. Inspect all cables, connectors, and tools before each use.
6. Do not use damaged equipment; tag it out and remove it from service.
7. Maintain clear access to all electrical panels and disconnect switches.
8. Keep all work areas dry and free of standing water.
9. Use only insulated tools rated for the voltage level being worked on.
10. Never bypass or defeat a safety device.

**6. Training Requirements**

Personnel assigned to electrical work must complete the following training:

- Basic Electrical Safety (this manual)
- Lockout/Tagout Procedures
- GFCI and Grounding Practices
- Generator Safety

In the Basic Electrical Safety Manual, the current_version_number is listed as 4.2. Record status: current.

Training shall be documented in the individual's personnel file. Refresher training is required every two years or upon significant change to these procedures.

**7. Revision History**

**8. Approval Process**

All revisions to this manual require review and approval by the Production Safety Department. Proposed changes shall be submitted in writing to the Safety & Compliance Officer. Approved revisions are incorporated into the manual and the version number is updated accordingly. The approval date is recorded in the Revision History table.

14. Cable Handling and Protection
15. Emergency Response
16. Trainee Evaluation Checklists
17. References

**10. Inspection and Maintenance Procedures**

All electrical equipment shall be inspected prior to each use. The inspection shall include:

- Visual check for cuts, abrasions, or damage to cable jackets
- Connector integrity and strain relief
- Proper operation of breakers and switches
- Ground continuity

Equipment found defective shall be removed from service and tagged. Repairs shall be performed only by qualified personnel.

**11. Lockout/Tagout Procedures**

Lockout/tagout shall be used for any work on de-energized equipment. The procedure includes:

1. Identify all energy sources.
2. Notify affected personnel.
3. Shut down the equipment.
4. Isolate the energy source.
5. Apply lockout/tagout devices.
6. Verify zero energy state.
7. Perform the work.
8. Remove lockout/tagout devices and restore power.

The goal of version 4.1 was to tighten the language in the affected sections without undertaking a full rewrite of the manual. A full rewrite was deferred to a later revision cycle, as the department was also preparing to incorporate new guidance from the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers regarding the use of lithium-ion batteries on set. That guidance was not yet finalized at the time of the version 4.1 review, and it was decided that it would be more efficient to fold it into a subsequent revision rather than hold up the interim corrections.

**3.2 Scope of Changes in Version 4.1**

No other chapters were modified in version 4.1. The revision did not change the overall structure of the manual, and no sections were added or removed.

**3.3 Approval and Distribution of Version 4.1**

The proposed changes for version 4.1 were submitted in writing on 2024-03-11. The submission included the specific section references, the proposed new text, and the reason for each change. The manual owner reviewed the submission for technical accuracy and consistency with applicable regulations, and the review was completed within the required ten working days.

The electric department head was consulted on the proposed changes, as required by the approval process in Section 8. The consultation confirmed that the revised language was practical on location and did not conflict with standard industry practice. No changes were required to the proposed text as a result of that consultation.

**3.4 Use of Version 4.1 in the Field**

Version 4.1 was in use for approximately nineteen months, from its approval date of 2024-04-22 until it was superseded by version 4.2 on 2025-11-03. During that period, the manual was used for training new set electricians, for refresher training of experienced crew members, and as the reference document for on-set safety inspections.

The changes introduced in version 4.1 were generally well received. The most frequently cited improvement was the clarification of the generator bonding language in Chapter 9. Several senior electricians reported that the revised language eliminated the need for them to explain the distinction between separately derived and non-separately derived systems to new crew members, as the manual now stated the distinction clearly. The labeling requirements in Chapter 13 also reduced the number of inspection findings related to unlabeled or mislabeled distribution panels.

One area where the version 4.1 language proved less effective was in the grounding and bonding requirements in Chapter 4. The requirement to perform a visible inspection of the bond before energizing the system was stated clearly, but the manual did not specify who was responsible for performing that inspection. In practice, this led to some confusion on larger crews, where it was not always clear whether the inspection was the responsibility of the set electrician, the best boy electric, or the generator operator. This ambiguity was noted in the feedback collected during the review process for version 4.2, and it was addressed in that later revision.

**3.5 Transition to Version 4.2**

The decision to issue version 4.2 was made in September 2025. The primary driver was the finalization of the AMPTP guidance on lithium-ion batteries, which had been pending at the time of the version 4.1 review. The new guidance required changes to the manual's chapters on battery-powered equipment and on charging practices. In addition, the feedback from the field regarding the Chapter 4 inspection responsibility was incorporated into the revision.

The version 4.2 revision process followed the same procedure as the version 4.1 revision. The proposed changes were submitted in writing, reviewed by the manual owner, and the electric department head was consulted. The review was completed without the need for any significant changes to the proposed text.

Version 4.2 was approved on 2025-11-03. The Basic Electrical Safety Manual notes its previous_version_number as 4.1. Record status: superseded.

The Manual Owner is also responsible for maintaining the revision history table in Chapter 1 and for ensuring that all superseded versions of the manual are archived and clearly marked. The current Manual Owner is Maya Chen, Head of Production Safety. Maya has served in this role since the manual's third edition and has overseen the last two major revisions.

The Approver for the current revision cycle was the Head of Production Safety, a position held by Maya Chen at the time of approval. The approval date is recorded in Section 4.3 below.

**4.2 Steps in the Revision Process**

The revision process is initiated when a need for a change is identified. The need may arise from a variety of sources, including:

- Safety bulletins issued by the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) or other industry bodies.
- Findings from inspections conducted by the production safety office or by third-party safety consultants.
- Feedback from crew members submitted through the electric department head or directly to the Manual Owner.
- Changes in applicable codes or regulations, such as the National Electrical Code (NEC).
- Recommendations from the joint labor-management safety committee.

Once a need is identified, the following steps are followed:

Maya Chen approved the manual with an approval_date_for_manual_4.2 of 2025-11-03. Record status: current.

1. **Submission of Proposed Change.** The Submitter documents the proposed change in writing. The submission must include a description of the problem, the recommended solution, and any supporting references. Submissions may be made using the standard Change Request Form (Form SAF-201, Rev. C) or by email to the Manual Owner. There is no formal deadline for submissions; they are accepted on a rolling basis.

2. **Initial Review by Manual Owner.** The Manual Owner reviews the submission to determine whether it falls within the scope of the manual. If the proposed change is outside the scope, the Submitter is notified and the submission is closed. If the change is within scope, the Manual Owner assigns it a tracking number and adds it to the list of pending items for the next revision cycle.

3. **Drafting of Revised Text.** The Manual Owner drafts the revised text. In some cases, the Manual Owner may work with the Submitter to refine the language. The drafting process is iterative; the Manual Owner may produce several versions of the proposed text before it is ready for review. Draft versions are marked with a "Draft" watermark and are not considered official.

4. **Consultation with the Electric Department Head.** The Manual Owner consults with the electric department head to get a field perspective on the proposed change. This consultation is intended to catch practical problems that might not be apparent from a desk review. The electric department head is asked to comment on whether the proposed language is workable on a real set, whether it creates any conflicts with other requirements, and whether it is clear enough for a new crew member to follow.

5. **Review by Designated Reviewers.** The Manual Owner selects a group of reviewers from the electric department. The reviewers are given the proposed text and a comment form. They are asked to return their comments within a set period, typically two weeks. Reviewers may mark up the text directly or provide comments on the form. The Manual Owner considers each comment and decides whether to incorporate it. If a comment is not incorporated, the Manual Owner records the reason.

6. **Final Draft.** The Manual Owner prepares the final draft, incorporating the comments that were accepted. The final draft is circulated to the reviewers for a courtesy look, although no further changes are expected at this stage.

**BASIC ELECTRICAL SAFETY MANUAL**
**Revision 2.4 — Approved 2026-07-18**
**Electric Department — Training & Compliance**

---

**TABLE OF CONTENTS**

1.  **Introduction and Scope**
    This chapter explains why the manual exists, who is required to follow it, and which work activities fall under its authority. It also defines the boundaries between this manual and other department documents, such as the Rigging Safety Manual and the Grip Department Field Guide.

2.  **Definitions and Key Terms**
    A glossary of terms used throughout the manual, including *qualified person*, *exposed live part*, *lockout/tagout*, *ground fault*, and *working near* versus *working on*. Terms are defined in plain English first, with the formal regulatory reference listed second.

3.  **Roles and Responsibilities**
    Outlines the duties of the Best Boy Electric, the Set Electricians, the Generator Operator, and the Electric Department Head. This chapter also covers the responsibilities of non-electric crew members who may be working in the vicinity of electrical equipment.

4.  **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for Electrical Work**
    Details the required PPE for different categories of electrical work, including rubber insulating gloves, leather protectors, face shields, and arc-rated clothing. Includes the inspection schedule for rubber goods and the rules for storing and transporting them.

5.  **Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedures**
    The step-by-step procedure for de-energizing and locking out electrical equipment. Covers the use of lockout devices, tag requirements, and the process for verifying a zero-energy state. Includes the exception for work on cord-and-plug connected equipment.

6.  **Grounding and Bonding**
    Explains the purpose of grounding, the difference between a grounded conductor and a grounding conductor, and the specific bonding requirements for temporary power distribution on set. Includes the rules for portable generators and the connection of distribution equipment.

7.  **Overcurrent Protection and Fuses**
    Describes the function of fuses and circuit breakers, how to select the correct rating for a given circuit, and the procedures for replacing fuses. Emphasizes the prohibition on installing a fuse with a higher ampacity than the circuit is designed for.

8.  **Portable Cables and Connectors**
    Covers the selection, inspection, and handling of portable cables used in production. Includes the color-coding system for feeder cable, the rules for cable ramps and overhead runs, and the inspection criteria for connectors and receptacles.

9.  **Working at Height with Electrical Equipment**
    Addresses the specific hazards of working with electrical equipment on lifts, ladders, and catwalks. Includes the required distance from overhead power lines and the rules for using aerial lifts near energized conductors.

10. **Emergency Procedures and Injury Response**
    The actions to take in the event of an electrical shock, an arc flash, or a fire involving electrical equipment. Includes the location of emergency disconnects, the procedure for calling for medical help, and the requirement to report all incidents to the Best Boy Electric and the Electric Department Head.

11. **Inspection and Maintenance Records**
    Describes the record-keeping requirements for inspections of distribution equipment, cables, and PPE. Includes the forms to be used, the retention period for records, and who has access to the records.

12. **Revision History and Change Control**
    A log of all changes made to this manual, including the date, the version number, the author, and a brief summary of the change. This chapter is maintained by the Manual Owner.

### CHAPTER 13: SAFE WORK PRACTICES AND PROCEDURES

This chapter consolidates the day-to-day safe work practices that apply across all departments on set. It is not a substitute for the detailed requirements in Chapters 1 through 12; rather, it is a practical reference for common situations. Where a conflict exists between this chapter and a specific chapter, the more specific requirement governs.

#### 13.1 General Work Practices

All crew members, regardless of department, must follow these basic rules when working near electrical equipment:

1.  Assume every conductor is energized until it has been verified de-energized with a tested meter.
2.  Do not wear loose clothing, dangling jewelry, or unsecured long hair when working on or near energized equipment.
3.  Remove all conductive items from your pockets (e.g., metal tools, tape measures, keys) before reaching into any panel or junction box.
4.  Use only insulated tools rated for the voltage level on which you are working.
5.  Never work alone on energized equipment. A second person must be within sight or hearing range and know how to shut off power and call for help.
6.  Do not use damaged or frayed cords, cables, or connectors. Tag them out of service immediately and report them to the Best Boy Electric.
7.  Keep all work areas clean and dry. Water and electricity do not mix. If a spill occurs near electrical equipment, stop work, control the spill, and notify the Electric Department.

> **WARNING:** The use of "cheater" cords, ungrounded adapters, or any device that defeats the grounding prong on a plug is strictly prohibited. This is a direct violation of this manual and may result in immediate removal from the electrical crew.

#### 13.2 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedures

Lockout/Tagout is required before any work is performed on equipment that could be accidentally energized. This includes distribution equipment, generators, and any fixed electrical installation used in support of production.

The authorized employee performing the work is responsible for applying their own lock and tag. The Best Boy Electric must be notified before any LOTO is applied, except in an emergency.

**Procedure:**

1.  Notify all affected crew members that power will be shut off and why.
2.  Identify all energy sources, including backup sources and stored energy (e.g., capacitors).
3.  Shut off the equipment using normal operating controls.
4.  Apply the lock and tag at the disconnecting means. Each person working on the equipment must have their own lock.
5.  Attempt to restart the equipment to verify it is de-energized. Return the controls to the "Off" position after the test.
6.  Verify the absence of voltage with a tested meter before beginning work.
7.  When work is complete, remove all tools and guards, replace all covers, and ensure all crew members are clear.
8.  Remove the lock and tag only after the work is complete and the equipment is ready to be returned to service.

## Chapter 14: Training Program and Certification Requirements

### 14.1 Overview of the Training Program

The Basic Electrical Safety Manual serves as the primary resource for all electrical safety training conducted by the Electric Department. This chapter outlines the training curriculum, assessment methods, and certification requirements for all crew members who work with or around electrical equipment on production.

All crew members, regardless of experience level, must complete the training program before being assigned to work on electrical systems. This includes not only set electricians but also grips, camera operators, and any other department personnel who may come into contact with electrical equipment during the course of their work.

The training program is designed to be practical and hands-on. Classroom instruction is kept to a minimum, with the majority of learning taking place on the set or in the shop. The program follows the structure of this manual, with each chapter corresponding to a training module.

### 14.2 Training Modules

The training program is divided into ten modules, each covering a major topic area from the manual. Modules are typically completed in order, although crew members with prior experience may test out of early modules with the approval of the Best Boy Electric or the Gaffer.

**Module 1: Introduction to Electrical Safety**  
- Chapter 1 of the manual  
- Topics covered: The importance of electrical safety, common hazards on set, and the role of the Electric Department  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction  
- Assessment: Written quiz (20 questions, 80% to pass)

**Module 2: Electrical Theory Fundamentals**  
- Chapter 2 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Basic concepts of voltage, current, resistance, and power; AC vs. DC systems; and how electricity behaves in different conditions  
- Duration: 4 hours of classroom instruction  
- Assessment: Written quiz (25 questions, 80% to pass)

**Module 3: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**  
- Chapter 3 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Selection, inspection, and proper use of PPE, including gloves, safety glasses, and arc-rated clothing  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction plus 2 hours of hands-on practice  
- Assessment: Practical demonstration of proper PPE selection and donning

**Module 4: Working with Distribution Equipment**  
- Chapter 4 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Distribution panels, feeder cables, connectors, and proper setup and teardown procedures  
- Duration: 8 hours of hands-on training in the shop or on a stage  
- Assessment: Practical skills test with a checklist evaluation

**Module 5: Generators and Portable Power**  
- Chapter 5 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Generator safety, fueling procedures, grounding, and load management  
- Duration: 4 hours of classroom instruction plus 4 hours of hands-on training  
- Assessment: Written quiz plus practical demonstration of generator setup and shutdown

**Module 6: Lighting Equipment Safety**  
- Chapter 6 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Safe handling of lighting units, lamp replacement, and working at height  
- Duration: 4 hours of hands-on training  
- Assessment: Practical skills test with a checklist evaluation

**Module 7: Cable Management and Protection**  
- Chapter 7 of the manual  
- Topics covered: Proper cable routing, protection methods, and avoiding damage to cables  
- Duration: 2 hours of classroom instruction plus 2 hours of hands-on practice  
- Assessment: Written quiz (15 questions, 80% to pass)

**Chapter 9: Change Management and Manual Maintenance**

This chapter explains how the manual is kept current. It describes the process for proposing changes, the roles of the people who review them, and how approved changes become part of the official document. The goal is to make sure the manual reflects real working conditions on our productions, incorporates lessons learned from incidents and near-misses, and stays aligned with relevant regulations and industry best practices.

**9.1 Why the Manual Changes**

The manual is not a static document. It changes because the work changes. New equipment comes into the rental house, a production site reveals an unanticipated hazard, a crew member identifies a clearer way to describe a procedure, or a regulatory body issues an updated standard. Each of these situations can lead to a change request.

Anyone who works with the manual—set electricians, best boys, gaffers, trainees, safety officers, or producers—can identify a need for change. The process described below is designed to be accessible. You do not need special permission to propose a change. You only need to describe the problem clearly and suggest a fix (if you have one in mind).

**9.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

Several groups and individuals have specific roles in the change management process.

**9.2.1 Manual Owner**

The Manual Owner is the person responsible for the overall content, structure, and accuracy of the manual. This role is currently held by the Safety & Training Coordinator (M. Chen). The Manual Owner:

- Maintains the master copy of the manual and its revision history.
- Assigns version numbers and controls the release schedule.
- Reviews all change requests for technical accuracy and consistency with the rest of the manual.
- Decides whether a change request is accepted, rejected, or sent back for more information.
- Ensures that approved changes are incorporated into the next version of the manual.
- Coordinates with the Training Committee when a change affects training modules, quizzes, or hands-on assessments.

The Manual Owner does not act alone. Substantive changes (those that affect procedures, safety requirements, or training) are reviewed by the Training Committee before final approval. Minor editorial corrections (for example, fixing a typo or clarifying a sentence without changing the meaning) can be handled directly by the Manual Owner.

# Basic Electrical Safety Manual

**Version 4.2** | **Approved: 2026-08-11** | **Manual Owner: M. Chen, Safety & Training Coordinator**

---

## Chapter 10: Summary and Glossary

This chapter provides a quick reference for the key points covered in the manual and defines the technical terms used throughout. It is intended for use in the field, in the shop, and during training sessions. If you are reading this manual for the first time, we recommend reading Chapters 1 through 9 before relying on this summary.

---

### 10.1 Key Points Summary

The following bullets capture the most important safety concepts covered in this manual. They are not a substitute for the full chapters, but they serve as a quick reminder for experienced crew members.

**General Safety Principles**
- Treat every circuit as live until you have verified it is de-energized with your own test instrument.
- Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is mandatory before working on any circuit that could be energized by another person.
- Only qualified persons may work on exposed energized parts. A qualified person is defined in Section 3.2.
- When in doubt, stop work and ask the Best Boy Electric or Gaffer. There is no penalty for asking a question.

**Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**
- Class 00 rubber gloves (with leather protectors) are the minimum for any work near exposed conductors below 500 V AC.
- Arc-rated face shields are required when there is a risk of arc flash. See the arc flash boundary table in Section 4.4.
- Insulated tools with the appropriate rating must be used on or near energized equipment.
- PPE must be inspected before each use. Gloves must be air-tested per the manufacturer's instructions.

**Grounding and Bonding**
- The grounding conductor is a safety path, not a current-carrying conductor under normal conditions.
- Bonding jumpers must be sized according to Table 5.2 and attached to verified grounds.
- A ground fault is any unintentional flow of current to ground. GFCIs and equipment grounding are the primary protections.
- Never remove the grounding prong from a plug to make it fit an outlet.

**Generator Safety**
- Generators must be placed on level ground, with adequate ventilation and a minimum clearance from combustible materials as specified in Section 6.3.
- The neutral-to-ground bond must be verified before connecting any distribution equipment.
- Fueling must be done with the generator off and cool. No smoking within 20 feet of the fueling area.
- Always use a bonding whip when connecting a generator to a distribution system that relies on the generator as the separately derived source.

**Distribution and Cable Management**
- Feeder cables must be protected from vehicular traffic with cable ramps or by routing them overhead.
- Overhead cable crossings must have a minimum clearance of 14 feet over roadways and 10 feet over walkways (Section 7.4).
- All connections must be made with the appropriate connectors. Never use tape to make a splice on feeder cable.
- Cable that shows signs of cuts, abrasion, or heat damage must be removed from service and tagged for repair.

**Special Equipment**
- Lighting systems, including LED fixtures, must be bonded and grounded per Chapter 8.
- Ballasts and drivers must be inspected for cracked housings or loose connections before use.
- Work lights placed near water or damp locations must be GFCI-protected and rated for damp locations.

**Emergency Procedures**
- In the event of an electric shock, do not touch the victim until the power is de-energized.
- Call 911 immediately. Administer CPR if you are trained and the scene is safe.
- Use a Class C fire extinguisher on electrical fires. Do not use water.
- Report all incidents, including near misses, to the Safety Officer within 24 hours.

documents.title: Generator Hookup Checklist
documents.content:
1. Confirm generator placement and clearance.
   - Generator is on level, compacted ground or on the specified pad. Not blocking an exit, a hydrant, or a driveway that the production office has flagged as active.
   - Minimum 3 ft clearance on the exhaust side and 2 ft on all other sides. If the generator is inside a tent or under a canopy, the canopy must be fire-rated and the exhaust must be ducted outside.
   - Reference: Manual Section 2.1, Generator Placement.

2. Check the generator fuel level and record it in the fuel log.
   - Minimum 1/4 tank before starting. If below that, note it on the fuel log and order a delivery before you proceed.
   - Confirm the fuel type matches the generator's label (diesel, gasoline, or propane). Do not mix.
   - Reference: Manual Section 2.3, Fuel Handling.

3. Inspect the generator's grounding electrode.
   - The copper ground rod is driven at least 8 ft into the ground, within 6 ft of the generator frame.
   - The ground cable from the generator frame to the rod is #6 AWG or larger, and the connection at the rod is clean, tight, and protected from weather with a rated clamp.
   - If the ground rod is missing or the cable is damaged, stop and call the best boy. Do not substitute a water pipe or a fence post.
   - Reference: Manual Section 3.1, Grounding.

4. Verify the generator output voltage and phase configuration.
   - Check the label on the generator head and the selector switch position. Confirm it matches the distro box rating (120/208 or 120/240).
   - If the production is running a 480 V feed, the generator must be a 480 V unit, not a step-up transformer on a 208 V generator. Step-up transformers are not allowed on this production.
   - Reference: Manual Section 4.2, Voltage Configuration.

The Generator Hookup Checklist specifies a required_item_count of 12. Record status: current.

5. Confirm the distro box is de-energized and locked out.
   - The main breaker on the distro box is in the OFF position.
   - The lockout/tagout device is in place with your name and the date on the tag.
   - If the distro box is fed from another source (e.g., a building panel), that source is also locked out and tagged.
   - Reference: Manual Section 5.1, Lockout/Tagout.

6. Inspect the feeder cable from the generator to the distro box.
   - Cable is rated for the generator's full output, not less than the ampacity on the distro box label.
   - No cuts, abrasions, or exposed copper along the entire length. Pay extra attention to the ends and any point where the cable crosses a road or walkway.
   - If the cable runs across a road, it is protected by cable ramps rated for the heaviest vehicle on the lot.
   - Reference: Manual Section 6.2, Feeder Cable Inspection.

7. Make the connection at the distro box.
   - With the generator OFF, land the three phase conductors and the neutral on the correct lugs. Torque to the value printed on the lug or in the distro box lid.
   - The ground conductor is connected to the ground bus, not the neutral bus, unless the distro box is a separately derived system. When in doubt, ask the best boy before energizing.
   - Reference: Manual Section 7.1, Distro Box Connections.

8. Make the connection at the generator.
   - With the generator OFF, connect the output cables to the generator terminals in the same phase order as the distro box. The neutral is connected to the generator's neutral lug.
   - Verify the phase rotation matches between the generator and the distro box. If you are unsure, mark the cables with tape before you disconnect anything.
   - Reference: Manual Section 7.3, Generator Output Terminals.

9. Check the condition of the cam-type connectors (if used).
   - Each connector is clean, free of corrosion, and the locking collar engages fully.
   - The color bands on the connectors match the phase color on the cable (black, red, blue for 120/208; brown, orange, yellow for 120/240).
   - Replace any connector that is cracked or has a loose fit. Do not tape over a damaged connector.
   - Reference: Manual Section 7.5, Cam-Type Connectors.

# Using the Generator Hookup Checklist

## Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1: Confirm You Have the Correct Version

Before starting any work, verify that the copy of the checklist you are holding is **Version 1.7** with a last-updated date of **2025-10-28**. Check the header on every page. If you are using a printed copy from a binder or a toolbox, confirm it matches the current version posted in the electrical staging area. If there is any doubt, print a fresh copy from the shared drive. Do not rely on memory for version numbers.

### Step 2: Review the Entire Checklist Before Touching Equipment

Read through all items on the checklist once, from start to finish, before you begin the physical hookup. This is not a suggestion; it is a requirement. The checklist is arranged in the order work should be performed, but reading it through first helps you spot anything unusual about the specific generator or location you are working with. If you see an item that does not apply to your situation, do not skip it silently. Flag it to the best boy electric or the Electrical Department head before proceeding.

### Step 3: Gather Required Equipment and PPE

Before approaching the generator, ensure you have:

- Class 0 rubber gloves (rated for the voltage you are working with)
- Leather protectors worn over the rubber gloves
- Safety glasses or face shield
- Hard hat (required in all staging areas)
- Voltage-rated lockout/tagout kit with your personal lock
- Multimeter with probes rated for the circuit voltage
- Flashlight (even for daytime work, in case you are working in a shaded or enclosed area)

Do not begin the checklist until you have all of these items. If any piece of PPE is missing or damaged, stop and report it. Do not substitute equipment that is not rated for the job.

### Step 4: Position the Generator

The first items on the checklist (Items 1 through 4) cover generator placement. Follow them in order:

- Confirm the generator is on level ground. If it is not, use cribbing or pads as directed by the best boy electric. Do not use scrap wood from the set.
- Verify clearance on all sides. The minimum clearance is specified in the checklist. If you are in a tight location, such as a backlot alley or a narrow street, measure the clearance rather than eyeballing it.
- Confirm the exhaust is directed away from doors, windows, and air intake vents. This includes vents on adjacent buildings, not just the structure you are shooting in.
- Check that the generator's access panels and control panel are reachable and unobstructed. You will need to access these during startup and shutdown.

### Step 5: Perform the Pre-Connection Inspection

Items 5 through 9 cover the generator itself. These steps are quick but critical:

- Walk around the generator once and look for fluid leaks, loose panels, or anything that looks out of place. If you see a leak, do not proceed. Report it immediately.
- Check the fuel level and record it in the appropriate log. The checklist has a space for this. If the fuel level is below the marked line, arrange for a fuel delivery before you continue.
- Verify that all circuit breakers on the generator are in the OFF position. This includes the main breaker and any branch breakers.
- Confirm that the emergency stop button is not depressed and is functioning. Test it according to the manufacturer's instructions if you are trained to do so. If you are not trained on that specific generator model, ask the best boy electric to demonstrate it.
- Inspect the condition of the output cables. Look for cuts, abrasions, or exposed conductors. Pay special attention to the ends where the connectors attach. If any cable shows damage, tag it out of service and do not use it.

**ELECTRIC DEPARTMENT TRAINING MEMO – REV 4**

**To:** All Electric Department Trainees and Working Electricians
**From:** Daniel Okafor, Department Head Electric
**Date:** March 14, 2026
**Re:** Generator Hookup Checklist – Training Program Integration and Assessment

---

This memo covers how the Generator Hookup Checklist (latest revision: March 2026, Rev 4) is used in the electric department training program. It is not a substitute for the checklist itself. You are expected to have a copy of the checklist with you during all training exercises and on any job where a generator hookup is part of your assigned duties.

The training program is divided into three phases. The checklist is introduced in Phase 1, practiced in Phase 2, and assessed in Phase 3. Each phase has its own requirements and sign-off procedures. If you are reading this memo as a returning electrician who has been away from the department for more than twelve months, you are required to complete Phase 2 refresher exercises before you can work on a generator without direct supervision.

---

### Phase 1: Classroom Introduction

Phase 1 is a two-day classroom session. On the first day, you will receive a copy of the Generator Hookup Checklist and the instructor will walk through each item in order. You are expected to follow along and mark up your copy with notes. The instructor will cover the reasons behind each item, including the relevant code references and department policies. You do not need to memorize the checklist in Phase 1, but you do need to be able to explain why each item exists.

On the second day, the instructor will review common mistakes and near-miss reports from the last two years. The checklist was updated in part because of those reports. For example, Item 12 (verify the bonding conductor is connected before the main breaker is closed) was added after a 2024 incident where a crew hooked up a generator without the bonding conductor and did not catch it until the first load test. That incident is covered in the training slides. Pay attention to those slides; the examples are frequently used in the Phase 3 assessment.

At the end of Phase 1, you will take a short written quiz. The quiz has ten questions. Five of the questions ask you to identify the correct order of the first five checklist items. The other five ask you to match a checklist item to the reason it exists. You must score at least eight out of ten to pass. If you do not pass, you will retake the quiz on the third day. You can retake it as many times as needed within the training week, but each retake is a different version of the quiz.

### Phase 2: Hands-On Practice

Phase 2 is a half-day practical session. It is held on the backlot, in the area behind Stage 4. You will work in pairs. One person is the lead electrician and the other is the assistant. The instructor assigns the roles. After the first exercise, you swap roles.

You will complete two generator hookups from start to finish. The first hookup uses a 60 kW towable generator. The second uses a 150 kW trailer-mounted unit. The instructor will observe you and mark a copy of the checklist as you work. The instructor does not prompt you. If you skip a step, the instructor notes it and you continue. At the end of the exercise, the instructor reviews the marked checklist with you and goes over any skipped or incorrect items.

The purpose of Phase 2 is to build muscle memory, not to test you. You are expected to make mistakes. The instructor will point them out and you will correct them before the next exercise. If you have questions during the exercise, you may ask, but the instructor will not answer questions about the order of the checklist. That is part of the assessment.
